questions.stem: Where was Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Mexica (Aztec) Empire, built?
options: On an island in Lake Texcoco
High in the Andes mountains
On the coast of the Yucatán Peninsula
Beside the mouth of the Amazon River
questions.explanation: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in the 1300s on an island in Lake Texcoco, in the Valley of Mexico, linking it to the shore by causeways; Mexico City now stands on the site. The Andes were the home of the Inca, whose capital was Cuzco. Many Maya cities were in and around the Yucatán Peninsula.

questions.stem: What were the chinampas of the Mexica?
options: Stepped stone terraces cut into steep mountainsides for farming
Knotted cords used by officials to keep records of tribute
Stone temples built on the tops of great stepped pyramids
Garden plots built up from mud and plants in the shallow lake
questions.explanation: Chinampas were raised fields made by piling lake mud and plant matter inside fenced plots in the shallows, producing several crops of maize, beans and squash a year. Mountain terraces were an Inca farming method suited to the Andes. Knotted record cords were the Inca quipu.

questions.stem: What was a quipu?
options: A set of knotted strings the Inca used to record numbers and information
A Mexica book of painted pictures recording history, tribute and religion
A paved road that linked the far corners of the Inca Empire
The title given to the emperor at the head of Inca society
questions.explanation: The Inca had no writing system like Europe's, so trained record-keepers used quipus, cords with knots of different types and positions, to record census numbers, tribute and possibly other information. Painted books were codices, made by the Mexica and Maya. The Inca emperor was called the Sapa Inca.

questions.stem: Who was the Sapa Inca?
options: The emperor of the Inca, believed to descend from the sun god Inti
The chief priestess who looked after the great Temple of the Sun in Cuzco
The Spanish governor appointed to rule Peru after the conquest
The general who commanded the Inca armies on the frontier
questions.explanation: The Sapa Inca ('unique Inca') was the emperor, ruling from Cuzco and regarded as a descendant of Inti, the sun god, which gave him great religious as well as political authority. Spanish officials came only after the conquest. Atahualpa was Sapa Inca when the Spanish arrived in 1532.

questions.stem: What was the main purpose of the Inca road network, which stretched thousands of kilometres along the Andes?
options: To let traders pull goods in wheeled carts drawn by horses and oxen
To link Inca cities with Tenochtitlan for trade with the Mexica
To let merchants travel freely selling goods for gold and silver coins
To move armies, officials and relay runners quickly across the empire
questions.explanation: The roads, with rest houses and storehouses along them, let the state move soldiers and officials and send messages by relay runners called chasquis. The Inca had no horses or oxen and did not use wheeled transport; llamas carried loads. They also used no coins, and had no contact with the Mexica far to the north.

questions.stem: Why did the Mexica practise human sacrifice?
options: They believed offerings of blood and life repaid the gods and kept the sun moving
They believed it would frighten the Spanish invaders into leaving their lands forever
They used it as the method for choosing and crowning each new emperor
Spanish priests introduced it to the Mexica after the conquest of 1521
questions.explanation: In Mexica belief the gods had sacrificed themselves to create the world and set the sun in motion, so humans owed them offerings of blood and life to keep the universe going. The practice was centuries older than the Spanish arrival. Historians also note that Spanish writers sometimes exaggerated it to justify the conquest, so their numbers are treated with caution.

questions.stem: When Christopher Columbus sailed west from Spain in 1492, what was he trying to reach?
options: The great southern land of Australia
Asia, by a western sea route
The southern tip of Africa
The Americas, which he knew existed
questions.explanation: Columbus, sailing for Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Spain, hoped to reach Asia (the 'Indies') and its spice trade by sailing west. He landed in the Caribbean and believed for the rest of his life that he had reached islands off Asia. Europeans did not know the Americas existed, which is why he called the Taino people he met 'Indians'.

questions.stem: What did the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) do?
options: Banned the enslavement of Indigenous peoples throughout the Americas
Divided newly found lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal
Ended the war between Spain and the Mexica after Tenochtitlan's fall
Gave England and France the right to settle North America
questions.explanation: Following a decree by Pope Alexander VI in 1493, Spain and Portugal agreed in 1494 to a line running north–south through the Atlantic: lands west of it went to Spain and lands east to Portugal. This is why Brazil, which lay east of the line, became Portuguese. The treaty was made decades before the fall of Tenochtitlan, and other European powers ignored it.

questions.stem: The phrase 'Gold, God and Glory' is often used to summarise:
options: the motives behind Spanish exploration and conquest
the three most important gods worshipped by the Mexica
the names of the three ships of Columbus in 1492
the motto painted on the banners of the Inca army
questions.explanation: Historians use 'Gold, God and Glory' as shorthand for the conquistadors' motives: wealth, spreading Christianity and winning fame and status for themselves and Spain. Columbus's three ships were the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María. The phrase is a modern summary, not a slogan from the time.

questions.stem: In 1513, which Spanish explorer crossed the Isthmus of Panama and became the first European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Americas?
options: Ferdinand Magellan
Hernán Cortés
Christopher Columbus
Vasco Núñez de Balboa
questions.explanation: Balboa crossed Panama in 1513 and claimed the 'South Sea' for Spain. Magellan sailed into the ocean in 1520 and gave it the name Pacific, but he was not the first European to see it. Cortés led the conquest of the Mexica Empire from 1519.

questions.stem: Who was Malinche (also called Malintzin or Doña Marina)?
options: Moctezuma's eldest daughter, who ruled Tenochtitlan as empress after her father's death
A Tlaxcalan war leader who commanded the allied Indigenous armies
An Inca noblewoman who helped Pizarro find the treasure of Cuzco
A Nahua woman, enslaved and given to the Spanish, who interpreted for Cortés
questions.explanation: Malinche spoke Nahuatl and a Maya language and soon learnt Spanish, so she became Cortés's interpreter and adviser, and was vital to his dealings with Indigenous leaders. She had been enslaved before being given to the Spanish. In Mexico she was long called a traitor, but many historians now see her as a young woman surviving with very few choices.

questions.stem: Why did the people of Tlaxcala join Cortés against Tenochtitlan?
options: They were Spanish settlers who had already lived in Mexico for years
They were old enemies of the Mexica and wanted to end their power
They had become Christians before the Spanish arrived in 1519
Moctezuma ordered them to guide and protect the Spanish visitors on the road to Tenochtitlan
questions.explanation: Tlaxcala had stayed independent of the Mexica but was surrounded by them and often at war with them, so its leaders saw the Spanish as useful allies. Tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other Indigenous warriors fought in the siege of Tenochtitlan, far outnumbering the Spanish. Christianity reached them only after contact.

questions.stem: In which year did Tenochtitlan fall to Cortés and his Indigenous allies?
questions.explanation: Tenochtitlan fell in August 1521 after a long siege, during which smallpox had already killed many of its people, including the ruler Cuitláhuac. 1492 was Columbus's first voyage and 1532 was Pizarro's capture of Atahualpa. 1572 saw the execution of Túpac Amaru, the last Inca ruler.

questions.stem: How did a few hundred Spanish soldiers defeat the Mexica and Inca empires, according to most historians today?
options: The Spanish armies that landed were larger than any army the Mexica or Inca could raise
Neither empire had organised armies, fortifications or weapons of its own
Epidemics and huge numbers of Indigenous allies counted for far more than Spanish weapons
The Mexica and Inca believed every Spaniard was a god, so most refused to fight back
questions.explanation: Steel, horses and guns gave the Spanish advantages, but historians stress that smallpox killed huge numbers and that tens of thousands of Indigenous allies did much of the fighting, alongside divisions such as the Inca civil war. The story that the Mexica thought Cortés was the god Quetzalcoatl appears in accounts written decades later, and many historians now doubt it. Both empires had large, experienced armies.

questions.stem: What happened when Francisco Pizarro met the Sapa Inca Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532?
options: The Spanish ambushed and captured him, took a vast ransom and later executed him
Atahualpa defeated the Spanish force, which retreated back to Panama by sea
Atahualpa became a Christian and ruled Peru as a loyal governor for the King of Spain
The two leaders signed a treaty dividing the Inca lands between them
questions.explanation: Pizarro's men attacked Atahualpa's largely unarmed attendants in the town square and seized him. Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold and twice over with silver to be freed; the Spanish took the ransom but executed him in 1533. Killing the Sapa Inca threw the empire's leadership into confusion.

questions.stem: Why was the Inca Empire especially vulnerable when Pizarro arrived in 1532?
options: Its nobles had invited Spain to take over and end the rule of the emperor
An epidemic had killed the emperor, and his sons then fought a civil war for the throne
Its armies had recently been destroyed in a long war against the Mexica
It had no roads, so its soldiers could not gather quickly enough to face the invaders
questions.explanation: The Sapa Inca Huayna Capac died in the 1520s, probably of smallpox that spread ahead of the Spanish, and his sons Atahualpa and Huáscar then fought a bitter civil war. Atahualpa had only just won when Pizarro arrived. The Inca had no contact with the Mexica, and their road network was one of their great strengths.

questions.stem: How did the encomienda system work in the Spanish colonies?
options: Indigenous people were paid fair wages by Spanish settlers to work on whichever farms and mines they chose
Indigenous leaders granted land to Spanish farmers in exchange for horses, steel and guns
Spanish settlers paid yearly tribute to the surviving Inca rulers for permission to farm
Settlers got the labour and tribute of Indigenous people, supposedly in return for teaching them Christianity
questions.explanation: Under the encomienda, the Spanish Crown 'entrusted' groups of Indigenous people to a settler, who could demand their labour and tribute and was supposed to protect them and convert them. In practice it led to brutal exploitation, which critics such as the friar Bartolomé de las Casas condemned. Workers had no choice and were not paid fair wages.

questions.stem: What was Potosí, in today's Bolivia?
options: The island city that became the site of Mexico City
The Spanish port from which Columbus sailed in 1492
A huge silver-mining centre where Indigenous people were forced to work
The Inca capital in the Andes, where the great Temple of the Sun stood
questions.explanation: Potosí's 'Rich Mountain' produced enormous amounts of silver for Spain from the 1540s, using forced Indigenous labour under a system called the mita, and many workers died in the mines. The Inca capital with the Temple of the Sun was Cuzco. Columbus sailed from Palos de la Frontera.

questions.stem: Which list shows only things carried FROM the Americas TO Europe in the Columbian Exchange?
options: Horses, wheat, cattle and sugar cane
Potatoes, horses, coffee and maize
Tomatoes, wheat, cacao and pigs
Potatoes, maize, tomatoes and cacao
questions.explanation: Potatoes, maize, tomatoes and cacao (chocolate) were first grown in the Americas and transformed diets in Europe and beyond. Horses, wheat, cattle, pigs, sugar cane and coffee all travelled the other way, to the Americas. Diseases such as smallpox also went to the Americas, with devastating results.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the long-term impact of the conquest on the Indigenous peoples of the Americas?
options: Populations fell catastrophically, mainly from disease, yet many Indigenous cultures survive
Indigenous peoples were wiped out completely, leaving no descendants or languages today
Indigenous populations grew quickly because European doctors and medicine cured the old diseases
Little changed for Indigenous peoples, because Spain only ever controlled a few ports
questions.explanation: Historians agree that the Indigenous population fell catastrophically in the century after contact, mostly from new diseases, along with war, forced labour and hunger; exact figures are debated. But Indigenous peoples were not wiped out: millions today speak languages such as Nahuatl and Quechua, and their cultures continue. European diseases caused the collapse rather than ending it.

questions.stem: The Florentine Codex describes the conquest of Mexico in Nahuatl, from accounts given by Mexica elders to a Spanish friar in the decades after 1521. What makes it valuable, and what limits it?
options: It preserves Mexica memories of the conquest, but was recorded years later under Spanish direction
It is an eyewitness diary written by Moctezuma, but it covers only his own palace
It was written by Cortés himself, so it is accurate about battles but leaves out the Indigenous allies
It records the Inca view of the conquest, but it was translated badly into Spanish
questions.explanation: The Florentine Codex was compiled by the friar Bernardino de Sahagún with Nahua scholars and elders, so it records the conquest from a Mexica point of view, in their own language and pictures. Because it was gathered decades later, under a Spanish friar's direction, historians weigh it alongside Spanish accounts such as Cortés's letters. It is about Mexico, not the Inca.

questions.stem: Who was Túpac Amaru, executed by the Spanish in 1572?
options: The Spanish viceroy who founded the city of Lima
The last ruler of the independent Inca state based at Vilcabamba
The Mexica ruler who led the final defence of Tenochtitlan
The Inca nobleman who helped Pizarro capture Atahualpa at Cajamarca
questions.explanation: After the conquest, Inca rulers kept an independent state in the remote mountains of Vilcabamba for decades. Its last ruler, Túpac Amaru, was captured and executed in Cuzco in 1572 on the orders of the viceroy Francisco de Toledo, ending Inca resistance from Vilcabamba. The last Mexica ruler to defend Tenochtitlan was Cuauhtémoc, and Lima was founded by Pizarro in 1535.
